title: US Data Centre Developers Shift Focus to Existing Pipelines as New Capacity Additions Slow in Q1 2026
gist: US data centre pipeline additions fell 19% QoQ to 36 GW in Q1 2026, a third straight quarter of deceleration off the >60 GW Q3 2025 peak, as incumbents pivot from land-grabbing to maturing existing pipelines. Cumulative disclosed capacity is 331 GW with ~40% actively developed, utility commitments crossed 195 GW (26% of 2025 US peak load), and disclosed capex passed US$1 trillion — but the money is extremely concentrated and ERCOT commitments are 86% speculative while PJM carries the reliability mismatch risk.

themes.theme: Pipeline deceleration and the shift from new sites to pipeline maturation

insights.claim: 36 GW of new data centre capacity was added to the US pipeline in Q1 2026, a 19% decline from Q4 2025 additions and the third consecutive quarter of deceleration.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The rate of change in announced AI/data centre demand is rolling over — a leading indicator for power equipment, gas turbine and grid capex order books two to three years out.
insights.quote: The 36 GW added in Q1 2026 represents a 19% decline quarter-on-quarter, extending a sustained deceleration that has now run for three consecutive quarters.
insights.locator: Pipeline continues to grow, but at a slower pace

insights.claim: Quarterly US data centre pipeline additions peaked at over 60 GW in Q3 2025 before falling in Q4 2025 and declining further in Q1 2026.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Q3 2025 marks the announcement-cycle top; use it as the reference peak when judging whether later prints signal stabilisation or continued contraction.
insights.quote: Quarterly additions peaked at over 60 GW in Q3 2025, before falling in Q4 2025 and declining further in Q1 2026.

insights.claim: Cumulative disclosed US data centre capacity now totals 331 GW, of which only about 40% is under active development.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Headline pipeline GW massively overstates deliverable load — roughly 130 GW is the realistic active base, which is the number to use for power demand modelling.
insights.quote: Cumulative US disclosed data centre capacity now totals 331 GW, of which approximately 40% is under active development
insights.locator: Cumulative US disclosed data centre capacity

insights.claim: Established data centre developers are shifting focus to maturing their existing pipelines rather than adding new projects, in response to an increasingly challenging development and regulatory environment.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Slowing additions reflect a strategy shift and permitting friction, not necessarily weakening AI demand — distinguish the two before extrapolating a demand bust.
insights.quote: Established data centre developers continue to shift their focus to the maturation of their existing pipelines in the face of an increasingly challenging development and regulatory environment

insights.claim: Q4 2025 pipeline additions were revised upward from the 25 GW originally reported, reflecting lags in disclosure tracking as project activity continues to be captured after the fact.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Real-time quarterly prints systematically understate additions, so the current 36 GW figure will likely be revised up too — fade the first reading of any single quarter's slowdown.
insights.quote: Q4 2025 additions have been revised upward from the 25 GW reported at the time of our previous release, reflecting lags in disclosure tracking

themes.theme: Geographic concentration and the new-entrant land-and-gas land grab

insights.claim: Texas leads all US states in cumulative planned data centre capacity at nearly 100 GW, with Ohio holding second place.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Texas alone is roughly 30% of the national disclosed pipeline — ERCOT-exposed generation, gas supply and transmission names carry the most direct beta to data centre load growth.
insights.quote: Texas leads all states in cumulative planned capacity, now totaling nearly 100 GW, with Ohio maintaining its position as the second-largest market.

insights.claim: Massive data centre sites are being planned in Utah, New Mexico and West Virginia where land availability is the key draw, but only a small fraction of these projects have moved into active development.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Announcements in frontier land-rich states are the lowest-quality part of the pipeline; discount them heavily when sizing local utility load forecasts.
insights.quote: Massive sites are also being planned in states such as Utah, New Mexico and West Virginia, where land availability is a key draw, though only a small fraction of these projects have moved into active development.

insights.claim: New entrants to data centre development are competing on gas supply and land access rather than incumbency, targeting states such as Texas and Utah.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Access to firm gas molecules and cheap land is the new entry ticket for data centre development — a structural bid for midstream capacity in Texas and the Mountain West.
insights.quote: New entrants focused on gas supply and land access are targeting states such as Texas and Utah, but only a small fraction of those projects are under active development.

themes.theme: Permitting progress versus scale: the count-capacity gap

insights.claim: While 53% of US data centre projects have passed permitting phases, that cohort represents just 32% of total pipeline capacity, showing that the largest projects lag furthest behind on permits.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Permitting progress headlines flatter the pipeline; the gigawatt-scale campuses that actually move power demand are the ones still stuck in approvals.
insights.quote: While 53% of projects have now passed permitting phases, this cohort represents just 32% of total pipeline capacity, underscoring the gap between project count and scale.

insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Near-term realised MW per project will undershoot pipeline averages, so 2026 incremental load growth lands lighter than announcement data implies — the density surge is deferred, not cancelled.

themes.theme: Utility commitments: PJM reliability mismatch versus ERCOT speculation

insights.claim: Large load capacity with signed construction or electricity supply agreements now totals 195 GW, equivalent to 26% of 2025 US peak load.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Contracted large load equal to a quarter of national peak demand is the single most concrete number for sizing incremental US generation and transmission capex needs.
insights.quote: Large load capacity with signed construction or electricity supply agreements now totals 195 GW, equivalent to 26% of 2025 US peak load.
insights.locator: Utility Commitments Cross 195 GW

insights.claim: Capacity in advanced discussion phases with utilities expanded nearly threefold from 37 GW in Q4 2025 to 107 GW in Q1 2026, indicating early-stage projects are progressing toward signed commitments.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Pipeline maturation is accelerating even as new additions slow — the conversion funnel, not the top of funnel, is where the 2027-28 load growth is being locked in.

insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A structural supply-demand mismatch in PJM points to sustained upward pressure on capacity prices and power prices there — the clearest expression of the data centre power trade.

themes.theme: Capex concentration and falling unit costs

insights.claim: Disclosed capex tied to specific US data centre projects crossed the US$1 trillion threshold in Q1 2026, though the figure is heavily skewed by a small number of large, speculative developments.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The trillion-dollar headline is not an underwriting-quality number — a handful of speculative megaprojects drive it, so treat it as an announcement ceiling, not a spend forecast.
insights.quote: Disclosed capex associated with specific projects crossed the US$1 trillion threshold in Q1 2026, though the figure is heavily skewed by a small number of large, speculative developments.
insights.locator: Capex Breaks US$1 Trillion Milestone

insights.claim: Just 6% of US data centre projects account for 42% of total disclosed capex, showing how concentrated investment has become at the top of the market.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Cancellation or delay of a few hyperscale megaprojects would remove a disproportionate share of forecast spend — concentration risk for suppliers levered to single flagship campuses.
insights.quote: Just 6% of projects account for 42% of total capex, highlighting how concentrated investment has become at the top of the market.

insights.claim: Per-MW data centre costs declined in Q1 2026, continuing a reversal from H2 2025 highs, and per-square-foot costs also fell after spiking in 2025.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Unit-cost deflation means dollar capex totals understate physical build volumes — and it squeezes pricing power for equipment and construction suppliers that benefited from the 2025 cost spike.
insights.quote: Per-MW costs declined in Q1 2026, continuing the reversal from H2 2025 highs, and per-square-foot costs also fell following a spike in 2025.

insights.claim: Average building square footage is rising even as overall campus square footage declines, pointing to an industry shift toward fewer, larger and more capital-intensive facilities.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Consolidation into fewer mega-buildings concentrates interconnection requests and supplier awards — winner-take-most dynamics for the vendors on those campuses.
insights.quote: Average building square footage is rising even as overall campus square footage declines, pointing to a broader industry shift toward fewer, larger and more capital-intensive facilities.

themes.theme: Around-the-meter generation as the new power procurement default

insights.claim: A growing number of pipeline projects are disclosing around-the-meter generation strategies, with the trend most pronounced in Texas where strong gas supply, faster permitting timelines and a robust renewables market create favourable conditions.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Data centres are increasingly bypassing the interconnection queue by building their own generation — bullish for on-site gas turbines, solar and storage vendors and a structural bypass of regulated utility rate base.
insights.quote: A growing number of pipeline projects are disclosing around-the-meter generation strategies, and the trend is most pronounced in Texas

insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Gas takes the larger share of capacity per project while renewables match it on deployment count — the split quantifies how urgency favours firm gas but cleaner supply is nearly as widely adopted.

themes.theme: Regulatory complexity: speed-to-power versus firm power

insights.claim: Interruptible service options are being deployed by utilities, forcing data centre companies to choose between speed-to-power and firm power.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: The speed-versus-firmness tradeoff is the key mental model for how loads get connected — it creates demand for on-site backup generation and demand-response-capable assets.
insights.quote: Interruptible service options are being deployed, forcing companies to choose between speed-to-power and firm power

insights.claim: Policymakers tend to view firm electricity service as an unnecessary friction to interconnection, biasing the regulatory system toward interruptible connections.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: If firm service is treated as an obstacle, data centres must self-supply firmness — reinforcing the around-the-meter gas and storage build-out thesis.
insights.quote: Policymakers tend to view firm service as an unnecessary friction to interconnection.

insights.claim: Fast-track capacity interconnection frameworks are being designed to bring new generation online quickly ahead of an anticipated supply crunch, but it is unclear whether policy developments will ultimately help or hinder demand growth.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Connelly
insights.so_what: Policy is the main swing factor between a data centre power supply crunch and an orderly build-out; watch state-level fast-track interconnection rulemakings as the key catalysts.
insights.quote: It remains to be seen whether policy developments help or hinder demand growth, however, as policymakers seek to balance the often-competing priorities of affordability and speed to power.
